explanations.answer: Blood Saul shed killing the Gibeonites
explanations.explanation: That's what the LORD tells David: "It is because of the blood shed by Saul and his family, because he killed the Gibeonites." Saul was Israel's king before David. David didn't guess at the cause. He sought the face of the LORD and got a straight answer. When you're stuck, friend, asking the One who knows beats staring at the empty cookie jar.

explanations.answer: Idols the people set up in the land
explanations.explanation: The LORD never mentions idols here. He gives one cause: the blood shed by Saul and his family, because Saul killed the Gibeonites, a people who were not Israelites. David asked a direct question and got a direct answer. I think that kind of clear answer saves a lot of guessing.

Sheba son of Bichri, a Benjamite, did lead a revolt against David (2 Samuel 20:1-2), but that's not what the LORD points to here. He says the famine is "because of the blood shed by Saul and his family, because he killed the Gibeonites." Saul was Israel's king before David. Two big troubles, friend, but only one is the answer to this question.

Careful here, friend, because the text says the opposite. Israel had taken an oath concerning the Gibeonites, but "in his zeal for Israel and Judah, Saul had sought to kill them." So Saul, Israel's king before David, did not keep it. That's why the famine story starts where it does.

That's right. The Gibeonites, a remnant of the Amorites, had an oath made concerning them. But Saul, Israel's king before David, "had sought to kill them" in his zeal for Israel and Judah. The oath was on the books, and Saul went the other way.

explanations.answer: How he can make amends to them
explanations.explanation: David asks, "What shall I do for you? How can I make amends so that you may bless the inheritance of the LORD?" Notice he asks first and doesn't just announce a plan. The Gibeonites were the ones who had been hurt, so he lets them speak. Good leaders, friend, ask before they act.

David doesn't bring that up. The text says the Gibeonites were not Israelites, but a remnant of the Amorites, and David never questions it. His question is about making things right: "What shall I do for you?" It's a better question than a quiz about their family tree.

David doesn't ask where anyone lives. He asks the Gibeonites, "What shall I do for you? How can I make amends so that you may bless the inheritance of the LORD?" He wants to hear what would put things right. The Gibeonites are the ones who get to answer.

explanations.answer: Whatever you ask I will do for you
explanations.explanation: David says, "Whatever you ask, I will do for you." The Gibeonites had just turned down silver and gold, and David still left the door wide open. That's a big promise to make before you've heard the request. I think David wanted to hear them out fully.

explanations.answer: Then I have nothing else to offer you
explanations.explanation: David doesn't say that. The Gibeonites say they need no silver or gold and no one in Israel put to death for them, and David answers, "Whatever you ask, I will do for you." He's not throwing up his hands, friend. He's giving them the pen to write the terms.

explanations.answer: Then I will ask the LORD again
explanations.explanation: David had already sought the face of the LORD, and that's how he learned about Saul and the Gibeonites (2 Samuel 21:1). Now he's talking to the Gibeonites directly. His reply is "Whatever you ask, I will do for you." He puts the whole matter in their hands.

They ask that "seven of his male descendants be delivered to us." They're speaking of Saul, the man who consumed them and plotted to exterminate them from every border of Israel. This is a heavy request, friend. They want to hang them before the LORD at Gibeah of Saul.

explanations.answer: Half of the land Saul held
explanations.explanation: Land isn't what they ask for. They say, "let seven of his male descendants be delivered to us." It's a request for people, and a hard one. The text doesn't mention any land in their answer.

Servants don't come up in their request at all. The Gibeonites ask for "seven of his male descendants." They say it about Saul, the man who consumed them and plotted against them. It's a specific number and a specific group.
David agrees. He says, "I will give them to you." That's a short answer to a heavy request. It sets up what comes next in the story, and it's a hard one.

David does agree. After the Gibeonites make their request, the king says, "I will give them to you." He had told them, "Whatever you ask, I will do for you," and here he follows through. It's a heavy moment, friend.

explanations.answer: Because of his oath with Jonathan
explanations.explanation: The text says the king spared him "because of the oath before the LORD between David and Jonathan son of Saul." Jonathan was Saul's son and David's close friend. Back then the two of them said, "we have sworn friendship with each other in the name of the LORD" (1 Samuel 20:42). David remembered the oath, and that's the reason the text gives.

explanations.answer: Because the Gibeonites left him out
explanations.explanation: The text gives a different reason. It says the king spared Mephibosheth "because of the oath before the LORD between David and Jonathan son of Saul." It doesn't say the Gibeonites left anyone out. It's David's own promise that holds here.

explanations.answer: Because Mephibosheth was still a child
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about his age here. It gives the reason in one line: "because of the oath before the LORD between David and Jonathan son of Saul." Jonathan was Saul's son. David kept the promise he'd made to his friend.

The text says David took "the five sons whom Merab daughter of Saul had borne to Adriel son of Barzillai the Meholathite." Merab was one of Saul's daughters. Along with Rizpah's two sons, that makes the seven. Keep the names straight, friend, there's a lot of them.

Michal was Saul's daughter too, the one Saul gave to David as his wife (1 Samuel 18:27). But this verse names Merab. It says David took the five sons she bore to Adriel son of Barzillai the Meholathite. Two daughters of Saul, and only one of them shows up in this verse.

Dinah was Jacob's daughter (Genesis 30:21), way back in the days of Israel's earliest family, so she's not part of this story. This verse names Saul's daughter Merab. David took her five sons, along with Rizpah's two.

Two plus five is seven, and that matches what the Gibeonites asked for. The text says David took "the five sons whom Merab daughter of Saul had borne." Rizpah's two were Armoni and Mephibosheth. Together they make the seven.
Math check, friend: two plus three is five, and the Gibeonites asked for seven. The text says Merab bore five sons, so two plus five makes the seven. It's a heavy count in a heavy story.
Two plus four gets you six, and the Gibeonites asked for seven. The text says David took "the five sons" Merab had borne, along with Rizpah's two. So it's five, and that makes seven in all.

explanations.answer: At the beginning of the barley harvest
explanations.explanation: The text says they were put to death "in the first days of the harvest, at the beginning of the barley harvest." Harvest is usually a season of gathering, and here it marks a sorrowful day. Sometimes the Bible just tells us when, plainly. It's a heavy moment, so I'll leave it at that.

explanations.answer: At the end of the wheat harvest
explanations.explanation: The text gives a different time. It says they were put to death "in the first days of the harvest, at the beginning of the barley harvest." So it was the start of the harvest, and it was barley. It's a heavy part of the story.
The text doesn't say that. It says "in the first days of the harvest, at the beginning of the barley harvest." Barley, not grapes. It's a hard moment in the story, friend.

explanations.answer: Birds by day and beasts by night
explanations.explanation: The text says Rizpah "did not allow the birds of the air to rest on them by day, nor the beasts of the field by night." Rizpah was Saul's concubine, and two of the seven were her sons. She spread sackcloth on a rock and kept at it, day and night. I think this one hurts.

explanations.answer: Thieves by day and strangers by night
explanations.explanation: That's not what the text says. Rizpah, Saul's concubine, kept away "the birds of the air" by day and "the beasts of the field" by night. Two of the seven were her own sons. She sat on sackcloth on a rock the whole time.

explanations.answer: Soldiers by day and mourners by night
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention soldiers or mourners here. Rizpah, Saul's concubine, "did not allow the birds of the air to rest on them by day, nor the beasts of the field by night." Two of the seven were her sons. It's a quiet, heavy picture, friend.

That's right. The text says she kept watch "from the beginning of the harvest until the rain from heaven poured down on the bodies." That's a long stretch of staying put. The rain marks when her watch ended.

The text says her watch did end at a certain point. It says she kept it "from the beginning of the harvest until the rain from heaven poured down on the bodies." So she stayed until the rain came. It's a long time to keep going, friend.

The text says David "went and took the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan" from the men of Jabesh-gilead. Saul was Israel's king before David, and Jonathan was Saul's son. The text tells us this happened when David was told what Rizpah had done.
Samuel isn't mentioned in this part. David takes "the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan." He gets them from the men of Jabesh-gilead, who had taken them from the public square of Beth-shan.
Abner was Saul's commander (1 Samuel 14:50), but the text doesn't mention him here. David takes "the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan." Those are the two names in the verse.

The text says the opposite. After David brought the bones of Saul and Jonathan, "they also gathered the bones of those who had been hanged." So those bones were gathered too. The seven weren't left behind.

That's right. The text says, "they also gathered the bones of those who had been hanged." David had the bones of Saul and Jonathan brought from there, and the seven were gathered along with them. Nobody got left out.

The text says the bones were buried "in the tomb of Saul's father Kish." Saul and Jonathan went home to the family tomb in Zela, in the land of Benjamin. A family tomb is a quiet, settled place to rest.
Jesse was David's father (1 Samuel 16:1), not Saul's. This verse says the burial was "in the tomb of Saul's father Kish." Two fathers in the story, friend, and this tomb belongs to Saul's.
Ner is the name in "Abner son of Ner" (1 Samuel 14:50), but it isn't the name in this verse. The text says they buried the bones "in the tomb of Saul's father Kish." Kish was Saul's father.

explanations.answer: God answers their prayers for the land
explanations.explanation: The text says, "After they had done everything the king had commanded, God answered their prayers for the land." It started with David seeking the face of the LORD, and it ends with God answering. That's the story, from the first verse to the last.

explanations.answer: The Gibeonites move away from Israel
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. It says, "After they had done everything the king had commanded, God answered their prayers for the land." The Gibeonites aren't mentioned leaving. The last word goes to God's answer.

explanations.answer: Saul's family turns against King David
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that either. After they had done everything the king commanded, "God answered their prayers for the land." That's how the passage ends, friend, with God answering.
